claim: Neither pure end-to-end learning nor pure physics simulation alone suffices for deformable object dynamics; a hybrid approach combining a differentiable MPM simulator with learned residual correction and material inference achieves the best accuracy while preserving physical structure.

evidence.summary: The Abstract states: 'end-to-end learned alternatives extrapolate poorly and often violate basic physical structure' while 'existing approaches typically rely on per-object optimization to fit material parameters, which can be slow and cannot generalize.' The Introduction elaborates: 'Physics-based methods produce physically plausible motion, but they rely on material parameters that are hard to measure and must be recalibrated for each new object. Data-driven methods avoid this calibration, yet they are data-hungry and not guaranteed to respect physical law.' The Ablation (Section 5.3) shows: 'MfM alone is already a strong physics-grounded predictor, and adding RfD further reduces CD by 13.1% on elastic objects and 17.8% on elastoplastic objects.' The Related Work section explains: 'an analytical simulator never matches reality exactly: coarse discretization, simplified constitutive laws, and unmodeled contact and friction leave a persistent sim-to-real gap. This observation motivates residual-physics methods.'
